nodes.name: Matrix exponential action $E(t)v$
nodes.statement: We discuss the approximation of the matrix exponential, \begin{equation} E(t)v = {\rm e}^{\sigma\,t A} v, \quad A \in \mathbb C^{n\times n},~~\sigma\in\mathbb C, \end{equation} with step size $ t $, applied to an initial vector $ v \in \mathbb C^n $.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: The target is $E(t)v=e^{\sigma tA}v$ with step size $t$, matrix $A$, complex prefactor $\sigma$, and starting vector $v$.

nodes.name: Matrix exponential problem (2.1)
nodes.statement: E(t)v = {\rm e}^{\sigma\,t A} v, \quad A \in \mathbb C^{n\times n},~~\sigma\in\mathbb C,
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.label: exp(itA)v

nodes.name: Normalization $|\sigma|=1$, $\|v\|_2=1$
nodes.statement: To simplify the notation we assume $ |\sigma|=1 $ and $ \|v\|_2=1 $ without loss of generality.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error

nodes.name: Nonexpansive case
nodes.statement: We assume that $\mu_2(\sigma A)\leq 0$, where $\mu_2(\sigma A)$ denotes the logarithmic norm of $\sigma A$, or equivalently, $W(\sigma A)\subseteq \mathbb C_-$, where $W(\sigma A)$ denotes the field of values of $\sigma A$ and we will refer to this assumption as the \emph{nonexpansive case}.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: Assume the logarithmic norm of $\sigma A$ is nonpositive (field of values in the left half-plane); this is called the nonexpansive case.

nodes.name: Nonexpansive evolution bound
nodes.statement: $\mu_2(\sigma A)\leq 0$ implies $\|E(t)\|_2\leq 1$ for $t\geq 0$.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error

nodes.name: Skew-Hermitian case notation
nodes.statement: For the skew-Hermitian case with $ \sigma = -{\rm i} $ we write\footnote{In this case the matrix $ A $ is usually named $ H $ (Hamiltonian).} \begin{equation*} E(t)v = {\rm e}^{-{\rm i}\,t H} v, \quad H \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}~~\text{Hermitian.} \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: With $\sigma=-i$ the problem is written $e^{-itH}v$ with a Hermitian Hamiltonian $H$.

nodes.name: Unitary evolution in the skew-Hermitian case
nodes.statement: In this case, $ E(t) $ represents a unitary evolution, i.e., $ \|E(t)\|_2 = 1$.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
conclusions: $ E(t) $ represents a unitary evolution, i.e., $ \|E(t)\|_2 = 1$

nodes.name: Krylov subspace
nodes.statement: The numerical approximation of~\eqref{exp(itA)v} considered here (see~\eqref{Smv} below) is based on the conventional Krylov subspace \begin{equation*} \mathcal{K}_m(A,v) = \mathrm{span}\{v,A v,\ldots,A^{m-1}v\} \subseteq \mathbb C^n. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error

nodes.name: Arnoldi decomposition (Krylov identity)
nodes.statement: This produces a basis matrix $ V_m \in \mathbb C^{n \times m} $ satisfying $ V_m^\ast\,V_m = I_{m \times m} $, and an upper Hessenberg matrix $ T_m \in \mathbb C^{m\times m} $ such that the Krylov identity\footnote{ Here, $ {e_m = (0,\ldots,0,1)^\ast \in \mathbb C^m} $, and in the sequel we also denote $ {e_1 = (1,0,\ldots,0)^\ast \in \mathbb C^m} $.} \begin{equation} A\,V_m = V_m T_m + \tau_{m+1,m}\,v_{m+1}e_m^\ast \end{equation} is valid, with $\tau_{m+1,m}\in\mathbb R_+$ and $v_{m+1}\in\mathbb C^n$ with $\|v_{m+1}\|_2=1$.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: Arnoldi gives an orthonormal basis $V_m$ and upper Hessenberg $T_m$ with $AV_m=V_mT_m+\tau_{m+1,m}v_{m+1}e_m^*$.

nodes.name: Krylov identity
nodes.statement: A\,V_m = V_m T_m + \tau_{m+1,m}\,v_{m+1}e_m^\ast
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.label: krylovidentity

nodes.name: Lucky breakdown of the Arnoldi iteration
nodes.statement: We are assuming that the Arnoldi iteration is executed until the desired dimension~$ m $. Then, by construction, all lower diagonal entries of $ T_m $ are positive~\cite{saad03}. If this is not the case, i.e., if a breakdown occurs, it is known that this breakdown is {\em lucky,}, i.e., the approximation~\eqref{Smv} below obtained in the step before breakdown is already exact, see~\cite{saad92s}.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: Arnoldi run to dimension $m$ has positive subdiagonal; a breakdown is lucky and the approximation is already exact.

nodes.name: Krylov structure identities
nodes.statement: The following identities hold true due to the upper Hessenberg [tridiagonal] structure of~$ T_m $ together with~\eqref{krylovidentity}: \begin{equation} e_m^\ast\,T_m^{j}\,e_1 = 0 \quad \text{for}~~ j=0,\ldots,m-2, \end{equation} and \tjnew{ \begin{equation} A^{j}v = V_m T_m^{j} e_1,~~~0\leq j \leq m-1, \end{equation} see for instance~\cite[Theorem 2]{DK89} or~\cite{saad92s}.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
assumptions: the upper Hessenberg [tridiagonal] structure of~$ T_m $ together with~\eqref{krylovidentity}
conclusions: A^{j}v = V_m T_m^{j} e_1,~~~0\leq j \leq m-1,
nodes.statement_short: $e_m^*T_m^je_1=0$ for $j\le m-2$ and $A^jv=V_mT_m^je_1$ for $j\le m-1$.

nodes.name: Vanishing corner entries of powers of $T_m$
nodes.statement: e_m^\ast\,T_m^{j}\,e_1 = 0 \quad \text{for}~~ j=0,\ldots,m-2,
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.label: eTe

nodes.name: Krylov polynomial reproduction
nodes.statement: A^{j}v = V_m T_m^{j} e_1,~~~0\leq j \leq m-1,
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.label: HVTm

nodes.name: $\gamma_m$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, let \begin{equation} \gamma_m = e_m^\ast\,T_m^{m-1} e_1 = \prod_{j=1}^{m-1} (T_m)_{j+1,j}\,, \end{equation} where the claimed identity also follows from the upper Hessenberg [tridiagonal] structure of~$ T_m $.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: $\gamma_m=e_m^*T_m^{m-1}e_1$, the product of the subdiagonal entries of $T_m$.

nodes.name: Definition of $\gamma_m$
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.label: gammam

nodes.name: Standard Krylov approximation
nodes.statement: The standard Krylov approximation to $ E(t)v $ is \begin{equation} S_m(t)v = V_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,t T_m}\,V_m^\ast\,v = V_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,t T_m}e_1. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error

nodes.name: Standard Krylov approximation $S_m(t)v$
nodes.statement: S_m(t)v = V_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,t T_m}\,V_m^\ast\,v = V_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,t T_m}e_1.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.label: Smv

nodes.name: Krylov error operator $L_m(t)$
nodes.statement: We denote the corresponding error operator by $ L_m(t) $, with \begin{equation} L_m(t)=E(t)-S_m(t) \in \mathbb C^{n \times n}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error

nodes.name: Error operator $L_m(t)=E(t)-S_m(t)$
nodes.statement: L_m(t)=E(t)-S_m(t) \in \mathbb C^{n \times n}.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.label: Lerror

nodes.name: Defect operator
nodes.statement: We define the \emph{defect}\, operator $ D_m(t) $ of $ S_m(t) $ by \begin{equation*} D_m(t) = \sigma\,A\,S_m(t) - S_m'(t) \in \mathbb C^{n \times n}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error

nodes.name: Defect-based integral representation of the error
nodes.statement: L_m(t)v = \int_0^t E(t-s)\,D_m(s)v\,\mathrm{d} s.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: Variation-of-constants formula expressing the Krylov error as an integral of the propagated defect.
nodes.label: LDint

nodes.name: Explicit representation of the defect
nodes.statement: D_m(s)v &= \sigma\,A\,V_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,s\,T_m}e_1 - \sigma\,V_m T_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,s\,T_m}e_1 = \sigma\,(A\,V_m - V_m T_m)\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,s\,T_m}e_1 \notag \\ &= \sigma \tau_{m+1,m}\,\big(e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,s\,T_m}e_1\big)\,v_{m+1}.
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: The defect is a scalar multiple of $v_{m+1}$ with factor $\sigma\tau_{m+1,m}e_m^*e^{\sigma sT_m}e_1$.
nodes.label: Dm(s)v

nodes.name: Leading term of the defect
nodes.statement: D_m(t)v = \sigma \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\frac{(\sigma t)^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,v_{m+1} + {\mathcal{O}}(t^m),
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.label: Dm-lead

nodes.name: Orders of defect and error

nodes.statement: \noindent For any $ A \in \mathbb C^{\tjnew{n \times n}} $ the error $ L_m(t)v $ satisfies the asymptotic relation \begin{equation} L_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{(\sigma\,t)^{m}}{m!}v_{m+1} + R_{m+1}(t), \quad R_{m+1}(t) = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}), \end{equation} for $ t \to 0 $.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (leading error term)
nodes.statement: Taylor expansion. Due to $ L_m(t)v = {\mathcal{O}}(t^m) $, \tjnew{see~\eqref{orderofDmLm},} \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &L_m(t)v = E(t)v - S_m(t)v = \frac{(\sigma\,t)^m}{{m!}}(A^m v - V_m T_m^m\,e_1) + R_{m+1}(t),\\ &\text{with Taylor remainder}~~ R_{m+1}(t) = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}). \end{aligned} \end{equation} Multiplying the identity~\tjnew{{\eqref{HVTm}} (with $ j = m-1 $) by $ A $} and using~\eqref{krylovidentity} gives \begin{align*} A^m\,v &= A\,V_m T_m^{m-1} e_1 = (V_m T_m + \tau_{m+1,m}\,v_{m+1} e_m^\ast) T_m^{m-1} e_1 \\ &= V_m T_m^m\,e_1 + \tau_{m+1,m}\, (e_m^\ast\,T_m^{m-1} e_1)\,v_{m+1} = V_m T_m^m\,e_1 + \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m v_{m+1}, \end{align*} whence~\eqref{prop-3-proof} simplifies to~\eqref{asy-leading}. \qed
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error
nodes.statement_short: Taylor expansion of $E(t)v-S_m(t)v$; the $t^m$ coefficient is evaluated with the Krylov identity.

nodes.name: Taylor expansion of the Krylov error

nodes.name: Explicit Taylor remainder
nodes.statement: The Taylor remainder $ R_{m+1} $ in~\eqref{asy-leading} can be specified in a more explicit way showing its dependence on~$ m $, $$ R_{m+1}(t) = \frac{(\sigma\,t)^{m+1}}{m!} \int_{0}^{1} \big(A^{m+1} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,\theta\,t\,A} v - V_m T_m^{m+1}{\rm e}^{\sigma\,\theta\,t\,T_m} e_1 \big){(1-\theta)}^m\,\mathrm{d}\theta . $$

nodes.name: Error bounded by the integrated defect

nodes.statement: With $\|v_{m+1}\|_2 = 1$, and \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \delta_m(s) = e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,s\,T_m}e_1 = \big( {\rm e}^{\sigma\,s\,T_m} \big)_{m,1}, \end{equation} together with~\eqref{Dm(s)v} we obtain \begin{equation} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)| \, \mathrm{d} s. \end{equation} \end{subequations}

nodes.statement_short: Define $\delta_m(s)=(e^{\sigma sT_m})_{m,1}$; then $\|L_m(t)v\|\le\tau_{m+1,m}\int_0^t|\delta_m(s)|ds$.

nodes.statement: \delta_m(s) = e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,s\,T_m}e_1 = \big( {\rm e}^{\sigma\,s\,T_m} \big)_{m,1},

nodes.name: Hermite interpolation representation of matrix functions
nodes.statement: To approximate the error integral in~\eqref{errorapprox1} we use the representation of matrix exponentials via Hermite interpolation of the scalar exponential function on the spectrum of the matrix~$ T_m $, see~\cite[Chap.~1]{higham08}: If $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r$ ($ r \leq m $) denote the distinct eigenvalues of~$ T_m $ and $ n_j $ is the dimension of the largest Jordan block associated with~$ \mu_j $, then \begin{equation} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,t T_m} = p_t(T_m), \end{equation} where $ p_t(\lambda) $ is the {Hermite} interpolant of degree $ \leq m-1 $ of the function \begin{equation} {f_t}(\lambda) = {\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\lambda} \end{equation} over the nodes $ \mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m $ in the sense of~\cite[(1.7)]{higham08}, \begin{equation*} p_t^{(\ell)}(\mu_j) = f_t^{(\ell)}(\mu_j), \quad j=1,\ldots,r, \quad \ell=0,\ldots,n_j-1. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Degree of the Hermite interpolant is exactly $m-1$
nodes.statement: For a general matrix, the degree of $ p_t $ may be smaller than $ m-1 $. However, in our context a special case occurs: Since the lower diagonal entries of $ T_m $ do not vanish, $ T_m $ is nonderogatory, i.e., for each eigenvalue $ \mu_j $ the associated eigenspace is one-dimensional, see~\cite[Section~3.1]{horn85}. Then, $ \sum_{j=1}^{r} n_j = m $, which implies that the degree of $ p_t $ is exactly $ m-1 $.
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.statement_short: $T_m$ has nonzero subdiagonal, hence is nonderogatory, so the interpolant has degree exactly $m-1$.

nodes.name: Divided-difference representation of $\delta_m$
nodes.statement: \noindent Let $T_m \in \mathbb C^{m\times m}$ be an upper Hessenberg matrix with eigenvalues $ \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m $ and $ \text{spec}(\sigma T_m) \subseteq \mathbb C_- $. Then the function $ \delta_m(t) $ defined as in~\eqref{defdelta}, i.e., \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\,T_m}e_1 = \big( {\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\,T_m} \big)_{m,1}, \end{equation*} satisfies \begin{equation} \delta_m(t) = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m \leq {\frac{t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,\gamma_m,} \end{equation} with $ \gamma_m $ from~\eqref{gammam} and where $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t}$ is the {$ (m-1) $-th} divided difference over $ \text{\rm spec}(T_m) $ of the function $ f_t $ defined in~\eqref{def:thetadd}.
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
assumptions: $T_m \in \mathbb C^{m\times m}$ be an upper Hessenberg matrix with eigenvalues $ \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m $
nodes.statement_short: $\delta_m(t)$ equals $\gamma_m$ times the $(m-1)$th divided difference of $e^{\sigma t\lambda}$ over spec$(T_m)$, bounded by $\gamma_m t^{m-1}/(m-1)!$.
nodes.label: prop:prop1

nodes.name: Divided-difference identity and bound for $\delta_m$
nodes.statement: \delta_m(t) = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m \leq {\frac{t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,\gamma_m,}
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.label: deltam-repr

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (divided-difference representation)
nodes.statement: We proceed from the Newton representation of the interpolant $p_t(\lambda) $ from~\eqref{pt}, \begin{equation*} p_t(\lambda) = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{j+1}}{f_t}\,\omega_j(\lambda), \end{equation*} with $ \omega_j(\lambda) = (\lambda-\lambda_1) \cdots (\lambda-\lambda_{j}) $. {From~\eqref{eTe} and by definition of $ \gamma_m $, it is obvious that the $ \omega_j $ satisfy} \begin{equation*} e_m^\ast\,\omega_j(T_m)\,e_1 = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0, & j=0,\ldots,m-2, \\ \gamma_m,& j=m-1. \end{array}\right. \end{equation*} Together with~\eqref{pt} this shows that the identity claimed in~\eqref{deltam-repr} is valid: \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,t T_m}\,e_1 = e_m^\ast\,p_t(T_m) e_1 = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{j+1}}{f_t} e_m^\ast\,\omega_j(T_m)e_1 = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m. \end{equation*} According to~\cite[(B.28)]{higham08} the divided difference can be estimated by \begin{align*} &|f_t[\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m]| \leq \frac{\max_{z \in \Omega} D^{(m-1)}f_t(z)}{(m-1)!}\\ &\text{for convex $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb C$ which contains all eigenvalues $ \lambda_j$.} \end{align*} With $D^{(m-1)}f_t(\lambda) = (\sigma\,t)^{m-1} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\lambda} $, $ |\sigma|=1 $ and $\text{Re}(\sigma \lambda_j)\leq 0$ we obtain \begin{equation*} |\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t}| \leq \frac{t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}, \end{equation*} which implies the estimate~\eqref{deltam-repr} for $ \delta_m(t) $. \qed
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}
nodes.statement_short: Newton form of the Hermite interpolant plus the Hessenberg structure isolates the top divided difference; a cited derivative bound on divided differences gives the estimate.

nodes.statement: \noindent For the nonexpansive case the error $ L_m(t)v $ of the Krylov approximation~\eqref{Smv} to $ E(t)v $ satisfies \begin{equation} \| L_m(t)v \|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{t^{m}}{m!} \end{equation} with $ \tau_{m+1,m} $ from~\eqref{krylovidentity} and $ \gamma_m $ from~\eqref{gammam}.

nodes.name: Computable upper error bound

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (computable upper bound)
nodes.statement: We proceed from~\eqref{errestintdefect}. For $ \delta_m $ defined in~\eqref{defdelta}, Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} implies \begin{equation*} |\delta_m(s)| \leq \frac{s^{m-1}}{(m-1)!} \gamma_m, \end{equation*} and this gives an upper bound for the error integral~\eqref{errorapprox1}: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m \int_0^t \frac{s^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m \frac{t^{m}}{m!}, \end{equation*} which completes the proof. \tjnew{ Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} is applied here in the nonexpansive case ($ W(\sigma A) \subseteq \mathbb C_- $) which implies the requirement $ \text{spec}(\sigma T_m) \subseteq \mathbb C_- $, see~\eqref{subsetofspectrum}.} \qed

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (asymptotical correctness)
nodes.statement: The asymptotic estimate \begin{align*} \bigg| \| L_m(t)v \|_2 - \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{t^m}{m!} \bigg| &= \bigg| \| L_m(t)v \|_2 - \Big\| \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{(\sigma\,t)^{m}}{m!}v_{m+1} \Big\|_2 \bigg| \\ &\leq \Big\| L_m(t)v - \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m\,\frac{(\sigma\,t)^{m}}{m!}v_{m+1} \Big\|_2 = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}) \end{align*} is valid due to~Proposition~\ref{prop:prop3}, and this proves~\eqref{asyerrcorr}. \qed

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (bound for $\varphi$-functions)
nodes.statement: For $p=0$ the result directly follows from Propositions~\ref{prop:prop3},~\ref{prop:prop4} and Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp}. We now assume $ p \geq 1 $. Via the series representation~\eqref{defphiseries} of $\varphi_p$ we can determine the leading term of the error in an analogous way as in Proposition~\ref{prop:prop3}: \begin{align*} \varphi_p(\sigma\,t A)v - V_m \varphi_p(\sigma\,t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{(\sigma\,t)^m \,(A^m v - V_m T_m^m e_1)}{(m+p)!} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}) \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m \frac{(\sigma\, t)^m}{(m+p)!} \, v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}), \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{leadingtermphij}. Furthermore, proceeding from~\eqref{defphiint} we obtain \begin{align*} \varphi_p(\sigma\,t A)v - V_m \varphi_p(\sigma\,t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1}\big( {\rm e}^{\sigma\,\theta\,t A} v - V_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,\theta\,t T_m} e_1 \big) \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} L_m(\theta\,t)v \,\mathrm{d} \theta, \end{align*} with the error $L_m(t)v$ for the matrix exponential case. Now we apply Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp} to obtain \begin{align*} \| \varphi_p(\sigma\,t A)v - V_m \varphi_p(\sigma\,t T_m) e_1 \|_2 &\leq \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^m}{(p-1)!\,m!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^m \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^{m}}{(m+p)!}, \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{eresphij}. \qed

nodes.name: Asymptotic leading terms and $\mathrm{Err}_1$ for $\varphi$-functions
nodes.statement: From the representation~\eqref{defphiseries} for the $\varphi_j$ together with~\eqref{eTe} and~\eqref{gammam} we observe \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} e_m^\ast \varphi_j(\sigma t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{(\sigma t)^{m-1} e_m^\ast T_m^{m-1}\,e_1}{(m-1+j)!} + \mathcal{O}(t^m) = \gamma_m \,\frac{(\sigma t)^{m-1}}{(m-1+j)!} + \mathcal{O}(t^m). \end{aligned} \end{equation} By~\eqref{em-phi-e1} we observe $ e_m^\ast\varphi_{j}(\sigma\,tT_m)\,e_1 = \mathcal{O}(t^{m-1}) $ for $ j \geq 0 $ and we conclude that the asymptotically leading order term of $ L^p_m(t)v $ for $ t \to 0 $ is obtained by the leading term ($j=p+1$) of the series~\eqref{generalizeerrorSaadsum1}: \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} L^p_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t (e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+1}(\sigma\,t\,T_m) e_1 ) v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^m). \end{equation} Analogously we obtain the asymptotically leading order term of $ L^{p,+}_m(t)v $ for $ t \to 0 $ by the leading term ($j=p+2$) of the series~\eqref{generalizeerrorSaadsum2}: \begin{equation} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} (\sigma\,t)^2 (e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+2}(\sigma\,t\,T_m) e_1) \,A v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}). \end{equation} \end{subequations} The asymptotically leading terms in~\eqref{Lpleadingtermsum} and~\eqref{Lpplusleadingtermsum} can be used as error estimators: \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \|L^p_m(t)v\|_2 \approx \tau_{m+1,m}\,t |e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+1}(\sigma\,t\,T_m) e_1| \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \approx \|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2 |e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+2}(\sigma\,t\,T_m) e_1|. \end{equation} \end{subequations} The error estimators~\eqref{LPnextphierrorest} and~\eqref{LPplusnextphierrorest} are already suggested in \cite{sidje98,niewri12}. We will refer to them as $\mathrm{Err}_1$ in the context of the $\varphi$-functions with standard and corrected Krylov approximation, generalizing the corresponding quantities for the exponential case $p=0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (corrected approximation bound)
nodes.statement: Applying~\eqref{em-phi-e1} (with $j=p+2$) to~\eqref{Lpplusleadingtermsum} shows~\eqref{leadingtermphijcor}: \begin{equation*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\, \gamma_m\, \frac{(\sigma\,t)^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!} \,A v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+2}). \end{equation*} From Proposition~\ref{prop:generalSaadsum} we observe \begin{align*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \sigma\,t\,A \,\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v. \end{align*} Using the integral representation analogously as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi} for $L^{p+1}_m(t)v$ and formula~\eqref{LDint} for $L_m(t)v$, we obtain \begin{align*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v &= \sigma\,t\,A\,\, L^{p+1}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} A\, L_m(\theta\,t)v \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} {\rm e}^{\sigma (\theta t-s) A} A v_{m+1} \delta_m( s)\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{align*} With norm inequalities \tjnew{(note the nonexpansive case)} and Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we obtain \begin{align*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \,t\,\|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &\leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m\, t^{m+1}\,\frac{1}{p!\,m!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta ^m\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m \frac{t^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!}, \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{eresphijcor}. \tjnew{Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} is applied here in the nonexpansive case, see also the proof of Theorem \ref{theorem:upperboundexp}.}\hfill\qed

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (Hermitian case)
nodes.statement: For \tjnew{a Hermitian} matrix $A$ we obtain a symmetric, tridiagonal matrix $T_m$ with distinct, real eigenvalues via Lanczos approximation, see~\cite[Chap. 3.1]{horn85}. By Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we observe \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m \end{equation*} with $f_t(\lambda)={\rm e}^{t\,\lambda}$ for the case $\sigma=1$. For divided differences of real-valued functions over real nodes we obtain $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \in \mathbb R$ and \begin{equation} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} = \frac{D^{(m-1)} f_t(\xi)}{(m-1)!} = \frac{t^{m-1} {\rm e}^{t\xi}}{(m-1)!}~~~\text{for}~~\xi\in[\lambda_1,\lambda_m]. \end{equation} Equation~\eqref{ddreal} shows $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} > 0$ and with $\gamma_m > 0 $ we conclude \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) > 0,~~~\text{and}~~~|\delta_m(t)|=\delta_m(t). \end{equation*} We continue with~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1} in the case $p=0$: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)|\,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{sT_m} \,e_1 \,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m} t \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(tT_m) \, e_1. \end{equation*} For the case $p \geq 1$ we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi}. Using definition~\eqref{defphiint} for the $\varphi$-functions and resorting to the case $p=0$ we find \begin{align*} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{align*} Evaluation of the integral yields \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p-1)!\,(k+1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^{k+1} \, \,\mathrm{d} \theta \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p+k+1)!}\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+1}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1. \end{aligned} \end{equation} This shows~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1}. To show~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate2} we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:asymerrorpricorrected}: \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 = \|t\,A\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m} \,t\, \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{equation*} Using $|\delta_m(s)|=\delta_m(s)$ and evaluating the inner integral by the $\varphi_1$ function, we obtain \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,\frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{equation*} Evaluation of the integral analogously to~\eqref{partofproofphicor1}, \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+2}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1, \end{equation*} completes the proof. \hfill\qed

nodes.name: Step size iteration for Hermitian matrices
nodes.statement: In the case of a Hermitian matrix $A$ the matrix $T_m$ is symmetric, tridiagonal and real-valued which allows cheap and robust computation of its eigenvalue decomposition. The eigenvalue decomposition of $T_m$ is independent of the step size $\Delta t$ and allows cheap evaluation of $\mathrm{Err}_1$ for multiple choices of $\Delta t$. In this case we can cheaply adapt the choice of $\Delta t_j$ in an iterative manner before continuing to time step $j+1$: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \Delta t_{j,1}&:= \Delta t_{j-1}~~\text{or result of~\eqref{choosestepbyEralocal}},\\ \Delta t_{j,l}&:= \Big( \frac{\tjnew{\Delta t_{j,l}}\,\,{\rm tol}}{\mathrm{Err}^{[j,l-1]}}\Big)^{1/m} \Delta t_{j,l-1},~~~~~ l=2,\ldots,N_j,\\ \Delta t_{j}&:=\Delta t_{j,N_j}.\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} By choosing $\mathrm{Err}^{[j,l-1]}$ as an error estimate for the Krylov approximation of the $j$-th step with time step $\Delta t_{j,l-1}$. For $\mathrm{Err}^{[j,l-1]}$ we can use $\mathrm{Err}_1$ or estimates given in Section~\ref{sec:defectquad}. The aim of the iteration~\eqref{eq:stepsize2loops} is to determine a step size $\Delta t_{j,\infty}$ with $\mathrm{Err}^{[j,\infty]}={\rm tol}$. The convergence behavior of iteration~\eqref{eq:stepsize2loops} depends on the structure of the corresponding error estimate. In our practical examples this iteration converges monotonically in a small number of steps. This step size iteration can also be used for the case of non-Hermitian $A$ with the drawback of higher computational cost for the error estimate $\mathrm{Err}^{[j,l-1]}$ for every $j$ and $l$.

nodes.name: Cheap versus expensive error estimates
nodes.statement: Error estimates for the corrected Krylov approximation or improved error estimates such as the improved Hermite quadrature~\eqref{eq:improvedHermiteQuad} require additional matrix-vector multiplications. Instead of investing computational effort in improving the error estimate, one may as well increase the dimension of the standard Krylov subspace. For comparison we test the original Expokit code, the corrected Krylov approximation with error estimate $\mathrm{Err}_a^+$ and the improved Hermite quadrature~\eqref{eq:improvedHermiteQuad} with Krylov subspace $m-1$. Table~\ref{Table:ExpensivErrEstvsCheapErrEst} shows that a standard Krylov approximation with dimension $m$ leads to better results, although all considered versions use the same number of matrix-vector multiplications. Whereas Expokit, improved Hermite quadrature (i.H.quad) and $\mathrm{Err}_a^+$ imply higher cost for the error estimate, the other codes $\mathrm{Err}_a$, effective order quadrature (eff.o.quad) and $\mathrm{Err}_1$ use standard Krylov subspaces and do not spend additional matrix-vector multiplications on error estimates. } \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline m=10& \text{Expokit} & \mathrm{Err}_a^+ & \text{i.H.quad} & \mathrm{Err}_a & \text{eff.o.quad} & \mathrm{Err}_1 \\\hline t &0.6620&0.7828&0.5863&0.8346&0.8366&0.8368 \\ N & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 \\\hline \text{\#\,m-v} & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 \\\hline \|L_m^{\star} v\|_2/t & 4.1\cdot 10^{-09} & 8.8\cdot 10^{-09} & 1.0\cdot 10^{-08} & 9.8\cdot 10^{-09} & 1.0\cdot 10^{-08} & 1.0\cdot 10^{-08} \\\hline \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline m=30& \text{Expokit} & \mathrm{Err}_a^+ & \text{i.H.quad} & \mathrm{Err}_a & \text{eff.o.quad} & \mathrm{Err}_1 \\\hline t & 8.1900 & 9.5763 & 9.6591 & 9.7482 & 10.2378 & 10.2473 \\ N & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 & 10 \\\hline \text{\#\,m-v} & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 & 100 \\\hline \|L_m^{\star} v\|_2/t & 3.6\cdot 10^{-10} & 2.7\cdot 10^{-09} & 9.2\cdot 10^{-09} & 2.6\cdot 10^{-09} & 9.5\cdot 10^{-09} & 9.7\cdot 10^{-09} \\\hline \end{array} \end{aligned} \end{equation*} \end{table}

nodes.name: Convection-diffusion equation
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &\partial_t u = \Delta u - \tau_1 \partial_{x_1} u - \tau_2 \partial_{x_2} u,~~\tau_1,\tau_2\in\mathbb R,~~~u=u(t,x),~~t\geq 0,~~ x\in\Omega=[0,1]^3,\\ &u(0,x)=v(x)~~\text{for}~x\in\Omega,~~u(t,x)=0~~\text{for}~x\in\partial\Omega. \end{aligned}

nodes.name: Discretized convection-diffusion operator
nodes.statement: The discretized operator is given by \begin{align} &A=( I_{n\times n} \otimes (I_{n\times n} \otimes C_1) ) + ( B \otimes I_{n\times n} + I_{n\times n}\otimes C_2 ) \otimes I_{n\times n} )\in\mathbb R^{N\times N},~~~\text{with} \\ &~~~B=\tfrac{1}{h^2} \text{tridiag}(1,-2,1)\in\mathbb R^n,~~~ C_i=\tfrac{1}{h^2} \text{tridiag}(1+\mu_i,-2,1-\mu_i)\in\mathbb R^n,~~i=1,2,\notag \end{align} and $\mu_i=\tau_i\,(h/2)$.

nodes.name: Taylor expansion of the error
nodes.statement: Taylor expansion. Due to $ L_m(t)v = {\mathcal{O}}(t^m) $, \tjnew{see~\eqref{orderofDmLm},} \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &L_m(t)v = E(t)v - S_m(t)v = \frac{(\sigma\,t)^m}{{m!}}(A^m v - V_m T_m^m\,e_1) + R_{m+1}(t),\\ &\text{with Taylor remainder}~~ R_{m+1}(t) = {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}). \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the error to order $t^m$ with Taylor remainder
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error

nodes.name: Evaluate $A^mv$ by the Krylov identity
nodes.statement: Multiplying the identity~\tjnew{{\eqref{HVTm}} (with $ j = m-1 $) by $ A $} and using~\eqref{krylovidentity} gives \begin{align*} A^m\,v &= A\,V_m T_m^{m-1} e_1 = (V_m T_m + \tau_{m+1,m}\,v_{m+1} e_m^\ast) T_m^{m-1} e_1 \\ &= V_m T_m^m\,e_1 + \tau_{m+1,m}\, (e_m^\ast\,T_m^{m-1} e_1)\,v_{m+1} = V_m T_m^m\,e_1 + \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m v_{m+1}, \end{align*} whence~\eqref{prop-3-proof} simplifies to~\eqref{asy-leading}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Use the Krylov identity to identify the $t^m$ coefficient and conclude
nodes.section: 2 Problem setting, Krylov approximation, and defect-based representation of the approximation error

nodes.name: Newton form of the interpolant
nodes.statement: We proceed from the Newton representation of the interpolant $p_t(\lambda) $ from~\eqref{pt}, \begin{equation*} p_t(\lambda) = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{j+1}}{f_t}\,\omega_j(\lambda), \end{equation*} with $ \omega_j(\lambda) = (\lambda-\lambda_1) \cdots (\lambda-\lambda_{j}) $.
nodes.statement_short: Write $p_t$ in Newton form with nodal polynomials $\omega_j$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}

nodes.name: Corner entries of $\omega_j(T_m)$
nodes.statement: From~\eqref{eTe} and by definition of $ \gamma_m $, it is obvious that the $ \omega_j $ satisfy} \begin{equation*} e_m^\ast\,\omega_j(T_m)\,e_1 = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0, & j=0,\ldots,m-2, \\ \gamma_m,& j=m-1. \end{array}\right. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Only $\omega_{m-1}$ contributes, with value $\gamma_m$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}

nodes.name: Divided-difference identity
nodes.statement: Together with~\eqref{pt} this shows that the identity claimed in~\eqref{deltam-repr} is valid: \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,t T_m}\,e_1 = e_m^\ast\,p_t(T_m) e_1 = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{j+1}}{f_t} e_m^\ast\,\omega_j(T_m)e_1 = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the identity $\delta_m=f_t[\lambda_1..\lambda_m]\gamma_m$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}

nodes.name: Cited divided-difference bound
nodes.statement: According to~\cite[(B.28)]{higham08} the divided difference can be estimated by \begin{align*} &|f_t[\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m]| \leq \frac{\max_{z \in \Omega} D^{(m-1)}f_t(z)}{(m-1)!}\\ &\text{for convex $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb C$ which contains all eigenvalues $ \lambda_j$.} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the divided difference by the max of the $(m-1)$th derivative
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}

nodes.name: Bound for $\delta_m$
nodes.statement: With $D^{(m-1)}f_t(\lambda) = (\sigma\,t)^{m-1} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,t\lambda} $, $ |\sigma|=1 $ and $\text{Re}(\sigma \lambda_j)\leq 0$ we obtain \begin{equation*} |\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t}| \leq \frac{t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}, \end{equation*} which implies the estimate~\eqref{deltam-repr} for $ \delta_m(t) $. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Left half-plane spectrum gives $|f_t[\cdot]|\le t^{m-1}/(m-1)!$
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}

nodes.name: Start from the integral bound
nodes.statement: We proceed from~\eqref{errestintdefect}.
nodes.statement_short: Start from the defect integral bound
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}

nodes.name: Integrate the bound on $\delta_m$
nodes.statement: For $ \delta_m $ defined in~\eqref{defdelta}, Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} implies \begin{equation*} |\delta_m(s)| \leq \frac{s^{m-1}}{(m-1)!} \gamma_m, \end{equation*} and this gives an upper bound for the error integral~\eqref{errorapprox1}: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m \int_0^t \frac{s^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m}\gamma_m \frac{t^{m}}{m!}, \end{equation*} which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Insert the bound on $|\delta_m(s)|$ and integrate
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}

nodes.name: Check hypothesis
nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} is applied here in the nonexpansive case ($ W(\sigma A) \subseteq \mathbb C_- $) which implies the requirement $ \text{spec}(\sigma T_m) \subseteq \mathbb C_- $, see~\eqref{subsetofspectrum}.} \qed
nodes.statement_short: Nonexpansiveness gives the spectral hypothesis of the proposition
nodes.section: 3 An upper error bound \tjnew{for the \tjnew{nonexpansive case} in~2.1}

nodes.name: Case $p=0$
nodes.statement: For $p=0$ the result directly follows from Propositions~\ref{prop:prop3},~\ref{prop:prop4} and Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp}. We now assume $ p \geq 1 $.
nodes.statement_short: Case $p=0$ reduces to the exponential results; then assume $p\ge1$
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Leading term via series
nodes.statement: Via the series representation~\eqref{defphiseries} of $\varphi_p$ we can determine the leading term of the error in an analogous way as in Proposition~\ref{prop:prop3}: \begin{align*} \varphi_p(\sigma\,t A)v - V_m \varphi_p(\sigma\,t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{(\sigma\,t)^m \,(A^m v - V_m T_m^m e_1)}{(m+p)!} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}) \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m \frac{(\sigma\, t)^m}{(m+p)!} \, v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+1}), \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{leadingtermphij}.
nodes.statement_short: Series representation gives the leading error term
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Integral representation of the error
nodes.statement: Furthermore, proceeding from~\eqref{defphiint} we obtain \begin{align*} \varphi_p(\sigma\,t A)v - V_m \varphi_p(\sigma\,t T_m) e_1 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1}\big( {\rm e}^{\sigma\,\theta\,t A} v - V_m\,{\rm e}^{\sigma\,\theta\,t T_m} e_1 \big) \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} L_m(\theta\,t)v \,\mathrm{d} \theta, \end{align*} with the error $L_m(t)v$ for the matrix exponential case.
nodes.statement_short: Write the $\varphi_p$ error as an integral of exponential errors
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Apply the exponential bound
nodes.statement: Now we apply Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundexp} to obtain \begin{align*} \| \varphi_p(\sigma\,t A)v - V_m \varphi_p(\sigma\,t T_m) e_1 \|_2 &\leq \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^m}{(p-1)!\,m!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^m \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,\gamma_m\,\frac{t^{m}}{(m+p)!}, \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{eresphij}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Apply the exponential bound inside the integral and evaluate the Beta integral
nodes.section: 4 Krylov approximation to $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Leading term
nodes.statement: Applying~\eqref{em-phi-e1} (with $j=p+2$) to~\eqref{Lpplusleadingtermsum} shows~\eqref{leadingtermphijcor}: \begin{equation*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m}\, \gamma_m\, \frac{(\sigma\,t)^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!} \,A v_{m+1} + \mathcal{O}(t^{m+2}). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Insert the expansion of $e_m^*\varphi_{p+2}e_1$ into the leading term
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Relate to $L^{p+1}_m$
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref{prop:generalSaadsum} we observe \begin{align*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v = \sigma\,t\,A \,\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Series identity $L^{p,+}_m=\sigma tA L^{p+1}_m$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Double integral representation
nodes.statement: Using the integral representation analogously as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi} for $L^{p+1}_m(t)v$ and formula~\eqref{LDint} for $L_m(t)v$, we obtain \begin{align*} L^{p,+}_m(t)v &= \sigma\,t\,A\,\, L^{p+1}_m(t)v = \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} A\, L_m(\theta\,t)v \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m} \sigma\,t \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} {\rm e}^{\sigma (\theta t-s) A} A v_{m+1} \delta_m( s)\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Express via the defect integral
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Bound the double integral
nodes.statement: With norm inequalities \tjnew{(note the nonexpansive case)} and Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we obtain \begin{align*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \,t\,\|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &\leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m\, t^{m+1}\,\frac{1}{p!\,m!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta ^m\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \|A v_{m+1}\|_2 \tau_{m+1,m} \gamma_m \frac{t^{m+1}}{(m+p+1)!}, \end{align*} which proves~\eqref{eresphijcor}.
nodes.statement_short: Norm bounds and the divided-difference estimate give the bound
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Check hypothesis
nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} is applied here in the nonexpansive case, see also the proof of Theorem \ref{theorem:upperboundexp}.}\hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: The proposition applies in the nonexpansive case
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Lanczos gives real distinct eigenvalues
nodes.statement: For \tjnew{a Hermitian} matrix $A$ we obtain a symmetric, tridiagonal matrix $T_m$ with distinct, real eigenvalues via Lanczos approximation, see~\cite[Chap. 3.1]{horn85}.
nodes.statement_short: Hermitian $A$ yields real symmetric tridiagonal $T_m$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Divided-difference form
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{prop:prop1} we observe \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) = \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \gamma_m \end{equation*} with $f_t(\lambda)={\rm e}^{t\,\lambda}$ for the case $\sigma=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the divided-difference representation of $\delta_m$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Mean value form
nodes.statement: For divided differences of real-valued functions over real nodes we obtain $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} \in \mathbb R$ and \begin{equation} \divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} = \frac{D^{(m-1)} f_t(\xi)}{(m-1)!} = \frac{t^{m-1} {\rm e}^{t\xi}}{(m-1)!}~~~\text{for}~~\xi\in[\lambda_1,\lambda_m]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Real divided difference equals a derivative value
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Positivity of $\delta_m$
nodes.statement: Equation~\eqref{ddreal} shows $\divdif{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m}{f_t} > 0$ and with $\gamma_m > 0 $ we conclude \begin{equation*} \delta_m(t) > 0,~~~\text{and}~~~|\delta_m(t)|=\delta_m(t). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\delta_m(t)>0$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Case $p=0$
nodes.statement: We continue with~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1} in the case $p=0$: \begin{equation*} \|L_m(t)v\|_2\leq \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t |\delta_m(s)|\,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m} \int_0^t e_m^\ast\,{\rm e}^{sT_m} \,e_1 \,\mathrm{d} s = \tau_{m+1,m} t \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(tT_m) \, e_1. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate $\delta_m$ exactly via $\varphi_1$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Case $p\ge1$
nodes.statement: For the case $p \geq 1$ we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:upperboundphi}. Using definition~\eqref{defphiint} for the $\varphi$-functions and resorting to the case $p=0$ we find \begin{align*} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &= \frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \|L_m(\theta\,t)v\|_2 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Integral representation reduces to the case $p=0$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Evaluate the integral
nodes.statement: Evaluation of the integral yields \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \| L_m^p(t)v \|_2 &\leq \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\frac{1}{(p-1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p-1)!\,(k+1)!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p-1} \theta^{k+1} \, \,\mathrm{d} \theta \\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{e_m^\ast \,(\,t\,T_m)^k \, e_1}{(p+k+1)!}\\ &= \tau_{m+1,m}\,t\,e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+1}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1. \end{aligned} \end{equation} This shows~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate1}.
nodes.statement_short: Series evaluation gives $\varphi_{p+1}$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Corrected error setup
nodes.statement: To show~\eqref{hermitianphiestimate2} we start analogously to Theorem~\ref{theorem:asymerrorpricorrected}: \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 = \|t\,A\,L^{p+1}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m} \,t\, \frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \int_0^{\theta t} |\delta_m( s)|\,\mathrm{d} s \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Start from $L^{p,+}=tAL^{p+1}$ bound
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Inner integral
nodes.statement: Using $|\delta_m(s)|=\delta_m(s)$ and evaluating the inner integral by the $\varphi_1$ function, we obtain \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,\frac{1}{p!} \int_0^1 (1-\theta)^{p} \theta \, e_m^\ast \, \varphi_1(\theta\,t\,T_m) \, e_1 \,\mathrm{d} \theta. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate inner integral via $\varphi_1$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Evaluation of the integral analogously to~\eqref{partofproofphicor1}, \begin{equation*} \|L^{p,+}_m(t)v\|_2 \leq \|A v_{m+1}\|_2\,\tau_{m+1,m}\,t^2\,e_m^\ast \varphi_{p+2}(\,t\,T_m) \, e_1, \end{equation*} completes the proof. \hfill\qed
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate analogously to get $\varphi_{p+2}$
nodes.section: 5 Corrected Krylov approximation for the exponential and $\varphi$-functions.

nodes.name: Peano representation
nodes.statement: It is useful to argue this also in a direct way: By construction, the Hermite quadrature formula underlying~\eqref{LDint-1-appr} is of order~$ m $, and its error has the Peano representation (cf. also~\cite{auzingeretal13a}) \begin{equation} \frac{t}{m}\,\Theta_m(t,t) - \int_0^t \Theta_m(s,t)v\,\mathrm{d} s = \int_0^t \frac{s\,(t-s)^{m-1}}{m!}\, \tfrac{\partial^{m}}{\partial s^{m}}\,\Theta_m(s,t)v\,\mathrm{d} s. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Hermite quadrature of order $m$ has a Peano kernel error representation
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited

nodes.name: Bound the derivative
nodes.statement: Here, $ \tfrac{\partial^{m}}{\partial s^{m}}\,\Theta_m(s,t)v = {\mathcal{O}}(1) $, because $ \tfrac{\mathrm{d}^{m}}{\mathrm{d} s^{m}}\,D_m(s)v = {\mathcal{O}}(1) $ which follows from $ D_m(s)v = {\mathcal{O}}(s^{m-1}) $.
nodes.statement_short: The $m$th derivative of the integrand is $O(1)$
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This shows that, indeed, the quadrature error~\eqref{quad-peano} is $ {\mathcal{O}}(t^{m+1}) $.
nodes.statement_short: Hence the quadrature error is $O(t^{m+1})$
nodes.section: 6 Defect-based quadrature error estimates revisited

nodes.name: Split time range
nodes.statement: We split the time range $[0,t]$ into $N$ subintervals, \begin{align*} 0&=t_0<t_1<\ldots<t_N=t, \\ \text{with step sizes}~~\Delta t_j&= t_{j}-t_{j-1},\quad j=1,\ldots,N. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Partition $[0,t]$ into $N$ substeps

nodes.name: Restarted Krylov steps
nodes.statement: Starting from $ \mw{0} = v $, for $ j=1,\ldots,N $, \begin{align*} \mw{j} := S_m^{[j]}(\Delta t_{j}) \mw{j-1} = V_m^{[j]} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,\Delta t_{j} T_m^{[j]}} \big(V_m^{[j]}\big)^\ast \mw{j-1} = V_m^{[j]} {\rm e}^{\sigma\,\Delta t_{j} T_m^{[j]}}e_1. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: For each substep build a new Krylov space from the current iterate and exponentiate
